capture.final_message:
Split the conjunction and prove stronger, independent statements.

- For the first conjunct, a finite flat module is finite projective. Hence \(M_{\mathfrak p}\) is a finite free \(R_{\mathfrak p}\)-module. Choose a basis at \(\mathfrak p\), represent the resulting isomorphism by finitely many elements and relations, and clear denominators. This produces \(a\notin\mathfrak p\) such that \(M_a\) is free over \(R_a\). Thus the hypothesis comparing ranks at maximal ideals is actually unnecessary.

- For the forward side of the `Iff`, use the standard local–global formula
  \[
  \operatorname{pd}_R(M)=\sup_{\mathfrak m\in\operatorname{MaxSpec}R}
  \operatorname{pd}_{R_{\mathfrak m}}(M_{\mathfrak m}).
  \]
  Localization gives one inequality. Conversely, over a Noetherian ring, finite syzygies remain finite; if the appropriate syzygy is projective after localization at every maximal ideal, then it is globally projective. This yields the reverse inequality, including the infinite-projective-dimension case.

- For the reverse side, prove directly that rank is locally constant on the free locus of a finitely presented module. If \(M_{\mathfrak p}\cong R_{\mathfrak p}^n\), finite presentation lets this isomorphism spread to some principal neighborhood \(D(a)\ni\mathfrak p\). Every stalk there is then free of rank \(n\), so the rank function is locally constant in the subspace topology.

Since both universal assertions in the `Iff` hold independently, each implication may simply discard its hypothesis and invoke the corresponding result. The essential finiteness assumptions are what permit local data—bases, presentations, and syzygies—to spread to neighborhoods or globalize.
